papers.title_in_file: A Highly Efficient and Pure Few-Photon Source on Chip
papers.version_note: arXiv:2309.15233v1 [quant-ph], 26 Sep 2023. The text layer holds the paper once; Tables I and II and several equations are flattened by the layer (exponents print as plain digits).
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper reporting a periodically poled lithium niobate microring that produces correlated signal and idler photon pairs by spontaneous parametric downconversion, measured with a two-channel photon-number-resolving SNSPD system for brightness, photon-number statistics, coincidence-to-accidental ratios, heralded g2 and mode purity.

assertions.value: The authors report an on-chip pair-generation brightness of 27 MHz/µW, obtained as the slope of a linear regression of the one-photon pair rate against on-chip pump power.
quotes: By linear regression, the brightness, defined as pair generation per unit pump power, is obtained as the slope of the fitting curve as 27 MHz/µW
the photons pairs are produced efficiently in single modes at rates reaching 27 MHz per µW pump power
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one device and one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 7 million pairs per second at 220 nW reported in the text equals about 32 MHz/µW as a single point, so the 27 MHz/µW slope is a fit across the power range, not that point.

assertions.value: The authors define the on-chip one-photon pair generation rate, to first order, as the product of the signal and idler single-channel rates divided by the signal-idler coincidence rate, and the two-photon pair rate as the product of the two-photon-per-channel rates divided by the two-photon coincidence rate.
quotes: the on-chip generation rate for the one-photon pairs is estimated to the first order as PSI = NSNI /NSI
the on-chip rate under first order approximation is PSSII = NSSNII/NSSII
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own estimators in the Photon correlation section.

assertions.value: The authors report that 220 nW of on-chip pump power creates 7 million one-photon pairs per second, and that the one-photon pair rate increases linearly with pump power.
quotes: As shown, PSI increases linearly with the power, as expected. Only 220 nW power is needed to create 7 million pairs per second.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the on-chip two-photon pair rate increases quadratically with pump power, which they attribute to the process being second order in SPDC, and give 8.6(104) at 220 nW and 9.5(106) at 1.12 µW as printed in the text layer.
quotes: here the rate increases quadratically over the power, because the underline process is of the second order in SPDC.
At 220 nW pumping, the two-photon pair on-chip rate is 8.6(104), and increase to 9.5(106) at 1.12 µW.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints 8.6(104) and 9.5(106) flat; they are most likely 8.6 times ten to the fourth and 9.5 times ten to the sixth per second, but the unit is not stated in the quoted sentence.

assertions.value: The authors report a second-harmonic generation efficiency of 0.33%/µW, from 75 nW of second-harmonic light coupled into the bus waveguide at 4.78 µW of on-chip pump power.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, p.2
quotes: With an on-chip pump power Pp of 4.78µW, PSH = 75 nW of second harmonic light is coupled out into the bus waveguide.
ηSHG = PSH/Pp2 = 0.33%/µW
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the pump power in the efficiency as Pp2, read as pump power squared.

assertions.value: The authors state the device is a periodically poled microring on a Z-cut lithium niobate on insulator wafer with a 600-nm thick film on 2-µm silicon dioxide, with a top width of 1.6µm and a radius of 80µm, coupled through a pulley bus waveguide.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, pp.1-2
quotes: with a 600-nm thick lithium niobate thin film bonded onto a 2-µm silicon dioxide layer above a sili-
a top width of 1.6µm and a radius of 80µm perodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) microring is etched with a pulley bus wavguide as the coupler
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own device setup (Device Calibration section).

assertions.value: The authors state that the calculated single-photon coupling strength g for the device is 2.98 MHz, using an effective nonlinear coupling expression (Eq. 2) taken from their earlier work.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, Eq. 2, p.2
quotes: For the current microring device, the calculated singlephoton coupling strength g is 2.98 MHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: A calculated value whose inputs are not listed in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state the effective Hamiltonian for quasi-phase matched, non-degenerate SPDC in a single-mode cavity, with signal, idler and pump annihilation operators and a nonlinear coupling coefficient g between the pump and the photon pairs.
quotes: In a single-mode cavity, the effective Hamiltonian describing quasi-phase matched, non-degenerate spontaneous parametric downconversion can be written as follows:
Hˆeff = ℏg(aˆsaˆiˆb†p + aˆs†aˆ†i ˆbp),
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model Hamiltonian (Eq. 1).

assertions.value: The authors state a visible pump pulse train with a pulse duration of 300 ps at a 10MHz repetition rate, exciting a quasi-TM visible mode at 776.96 nm of 1.14 GHz bandwidth, with signal and idler created at 1551.85 nm and 1555.93 nm, each of 1.68 GHz bandwidth.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, pp.2-3; Fig. 1
quotes: A visible pulse train with a pulse duration of τ =300 ps and a repetition rate of 10MHz is created with a bulk SHG system
to excite the quasi-TM visible mode at 776.96 nm with a bandwidth
of 1.14 GHz. There, signal and idler photons are created through SPDC into 1551.85 nm and 1555.93 nm quasiTM modes, respectively, each in bandwidth of 1.68 GHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The 300 ps pump pulse is chosen, per the paper, to match the cavity lifetime.

assertions.value: The authors report fiber-chip-fiber coupling losses of 9.2 ± 0.2 dB at 1553.93 nm and 11.5 ± 0.3 dB at 776.96 nm, PNR-SNSPD detection efficiencies of 70% and 82% with a dark count rate of 50 to 100 Hz, and total channel losses of 7.55 dB for the signal and 6.76 dB for the idler.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, pp.2-3
quotes: with the fiberchip-fiber coupling losses measured to be 9.2 ± 0.2 dB at 1553.93 nm and 11.5 ± 0.3 dB at 776.96 nm, respectively
feature a dark count rate of 50 to 100 Hz and detection efficiencies of 70% (corresponding to 1.55 dB loss) and 82% (0.86 dB loss), respectively.
the signal and idler channels experience a total loss of ηS=7.55 dB and ηI=6.76 dB, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own measured setup losses and detector specifications.
assertions.reader_inference: The 7 dB total channel loss is what limits the visible correlation of multiphoton states in this work, per the paper's own explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that an inline long-pass filter with an 80 dB extinction ratio and 0.5 dB insertion loss removes the pump, and that cascaded DWDM filters of 1.6 nm FWHM bandwidth with about 0.3 dB transmission loss separate signal and idler.
assertions.anchor: Device Calibration and Experiment Setup, p.3
quotes: the generated photon pairs are filtered using an inline long-pass filter featuring an 80 dB extinction ratio and a 0.5 dB insertion loss (IL)

cascaded dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) filters with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) transmission bandwidth of 1.6 nm are employed, resulting in a transmission loss of approximately 0.3 dB
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that the measured signal-channel photon-number distribution follows a single-mode thermal distribution for one and two photons at mean photon numbers of 0.0137 and 0.008, deviates clearly from a coherent distribution, and shows a noticeable discrepancy for three photons that they ascribe to SNSPD threshold sensitivity.
quotes: As seen, in both cases the measurement results agree well with TLD for the one and two photon cases. Compared with the coherent light distribution, there is a clearly deviation.
For the three photon case, there is noticeable discrepancy, which can primarily be ascribed to the threshold sensitivity encountered in higher photon situations for the present SNSPD system.
for two mean photon number cases: 0.0137 and 0.008
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical agreement judged from plotted comparison in one study; no fit statistic is given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no goodness-of-fit figure; agreement is stated from the plot.

assertions.value: The authors state the ideal single-mode thermal light distribution as P(n) = n-bar to the power n divided by (1 + n-bar) to the power (n + 1), where n is the photon number and n-bar its mean.
quotes: The TLD follows P (n) = n¯n/(1 + n¯)n+1, where n and n¯ denote the photon number and their mean, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the comparison distribution it uses.

assertions.value: The authors report normalized probabilities of detecting one, two and three photons of 2.80 × 10−3, 7.85×10−6 and 3.03×10−7 at a mean photon number of 0.0028, and 1.37 × 10−2, 1.91 × 10−4 and 1.77 × 10−6 at 0.0137.
quotes: when the mean photon number is 0.0028, the normalized probabilities for one, two, and three photons are 2.80 × 10−3, 7.85×10−6, and 3.03×10−7, respectively.
As we increase it to 0.0137, they each become 1.37 × 10−2, 1.91 × 10−4, and 1.77 × 10−6.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the multi-photon SPDC saturated regime starts at a mean photon number of 0.0137, so the three-photon probability shows no obvious increase there.
quotes: Because the SPDC saturated regime of multi-photon starts at mean photon number of 0.0137, there will be no obvious increasing at three-photon case.
assertions.certainty_reason: An explanation offered without a supporting model or measurement in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The 0.0137 value is also the largest mean photon number shown in Fig. 4, so saturation may reflect the detector (as the paper says for the three-photon discrepancy) as much as the source.

assertions.value: The authors report that joint photon-number probabilities inferred by loss inversion show signal and idler photon numbers that are correlated but not strongly, which they attribute to the high total channel loss (7.55 dB and 6.76 dB) and the low coincidence counts of multiphoton states, making the loss inversion not very accurate.
quotes: As seen, while the photon numbers in the signal and idler channels are correlated, the correlation is not strong.
because of which the loss inversion calculation is not very accurate.
This is mainly due to the high total loss of each channel (7.55 dB and 6.76 dB)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, with the paper stating its own inaccuracy.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says Fig. 6 is for 0.137 mean photon number on chip, while Fig. 6's caption gives a pump power of about 1.1 µW and the other mean photon numbers are 0.0137 or lower; 0.137 may be a typo for 0.0137.

assertions.value: The authors state that coincidence counts between S(n) and I(m) are events of detecting n signal and m idler photons in the same 400 ps time slot, and that accidental counts are events in a slot set 100 ns apart, over an acquisition period of 120 seconds at an average pump power around 1.1µW.
quotes: the coincidence rates between S(n) and I(m) are for event occurrences of simultaneously detecting n signal photons and m idler photons in the same time slot (in this case each of 400 ps width)
The accidental rates are for those events occuring in a different slot, set by 100 ns apart to avoid any correlation.
TABLE I. CAR measured at average power around 1.1µW
Over our total acquistion period of 120 seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its coincidence and accidental counts in the Photon correlation section.
assertions.reader_inference: The 120 seconds is stated as the total acquisition period in the sentence about three-photon pairs; the text does not say it applies to every Table I cell.

assertions.value: The authors report a coincidence-to-accidental ratio of about 10 for single-photon pairs and 100 for two-photon pairs at about 1.1 µW pump power, and for three-photon pairs record 3 coincidences and no accidental event over 120 seconds.
quotes: the coincidence to accidental detection ratio is about 10 for single-photon pairs, and 100 for two-photon pairs, which shows high correlation.
Over our total acquistion period of 120 seconds, we record 3 coincidence of three photon pairs, but no accidental event.
TABLE I. CAR measured at average power around 1.1µW
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the 3-event three-photon count is very small.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I in the text layer shows the S(1)I(1) entry as 1.84 × 10 to the sixth against 2.10 × 10 to the fifth (ratio about 9) and S(2)I(2) as 3.52 × 10 to the third against 35 (ratio about 100), consistent with the quoted ratios; the three-photon cell (3:0) has no finite ratio.

assertions.value: The authors report that the coincidence rates are not maximized on the diagonal; one signal photon with two idler photons is more likely than two signal with two idler photons, which they attribute to a total loss of about 7 dB per channel blurring the on-chip photon-number correlation.
quotes: the coincident rates are not maximized at diagonal. For example, the coincident detection of one signal photon and two idler photons is more likely than that of two signal and two idler photons.
the total loss is about 7 dB per channel so that only a fraction of them can be detected thus blurring the correlation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result with an explanation the paper does not test separately.

assertions.value: The authors state a non-classicality criterion gamma = g(1,2) divided by the square root of g(2,2) times g(0,2) that must exceed 1, built from the mutual correlation function g(n,m), and report gamma between 1.3 and 1.6 for pump powers from 220 nW to 1.12 µW.
quotes: To satisfy the non-classical criteria [3, 17], the following condition must be met: γ = g(1,2)/ g(2,2)g(0,2) > 1.
From the pump power ranging from 220 nW to 1.12 µW, we have calculated γ to between 1.3 and 1.6, indicating good quantum correlation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the criterion itself is cited from other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the square-root sign in the criterion; the form given in the value is the reader's reading of the flattened text.

assertions.value: The authors report an unheralded second-order correlation g2(0) of around 1.99 to 2.25 for the signal and idler channels, computed from the PNR-SNSPD photon-number distribution, which they say verifies thermal statistics under the single-mode condition.
assertions.anchor: Photon correlation, p.5; Appendix B, Fig. 10, p.6
quotes: The results are around 1.99 to 2.25 (see given in the Appendix B), verifying the thermal statistics of each SPDC channel under the single-mode condition.
As seen, for both channels gu(2n)c(0) ≈ 2 for each channel at different mean photon number.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: A single-mode thermal source has g2(0) = 2; a value of 2.25 is above that, and the text does not comment on the excess.

assertions.value: The authors report a heralded second-order correlation gH(2)(0) of about 0.01 at a mean photon number of 0.003 per pulse, rising to approaching 0.05 as the mean photon number increases, for both signal and idler channels, using the PNR-SNSPD photon-number statistics directly instead of a beamsplitter HBT measurement.
quotes: for both channels, gH(2)(0) is about 0.01 when the mean photon numbers are 0.003 per pulse and increases to approaching 0.05 as the mean photon numbers increase to
In contrast to standard Hanbury Brown and Twiss effect (HBT) measurement using a beamsplitter, here we utilize the collected multiphoton statistics directly by the PNR-SNSPDs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence breaks across the text layer at the page turn; the upper mean photon number, 0.014, is on the next text line.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that used as a single photon source the device gives heralded gH(2)(0) around 0.04 at a single photon rate of 650 kHz on chip, and in the introduction that the system can be used for heralded single-photon generation at 10 MHz clock speed.
quotes: Used as a single photon source, it gives heralded gH(2)(0) around 0.04 at a single photon rate of 650 kHz on chip.
we show how this system can be used for heralded singlephoton generation at 10 MHz clock speed.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract-level claim; the body does not state the 650 kHz figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The 650 kHz single-photon rate does not appear in the body text or captions read; the body reports gH(2)(0) of about 0.01 to approaching 0.05, which brackets 0.04 but does not tie it to a rate. The paper does not say whether the 10 MHz clock figure was measured or is the pump repetition rate.

assertions.value: The authors report an effective mode number K = 1/[g2(0) − 1] of 1.01, close to the ideal K = 1, which they state as a mode purity 1/K of 99 ± 4.9%.
assertions.anchor: Photon correlation, Table II, p.5; Abstract, p.1
quotes: the effective mode number K = 1/[g(2)(0) − 1] is at 1.01, which is very close to the ideal case with K = 1 [4].
This represents a mode purity of 1/K = 99 ± 4.9%, indicating an optimal condition for single mode photon production
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study with a stated uncertainty of 4.9%.
assertions.reader_inference: With a stated uncertainty of ± 4.9% the purity interval spans about 94% to above 100%, so the data cannot separate 99% from a modestly lower purity. The value g2(0) = 1.99 in Table II is below the 1.99 to 2.25 range reported in Appendix B at its upper end.

assertions.value: The authors compare, in Table II, their PPLN microring (300ps pump pulse, g2 1.99, K 1.01, purity 99%) with Eckstein, Harder and Stasi PPKTP waveguides at 1ps pump pulses (purities 95%, 89% and 99%) and a Si3N4 microring (Vaidya, 1.5ns pump pulse, 95%), as printed in the flattened text layer.
quotes: Eckstein[9] PPKTPa Waveguide Harder[4] PPKTP Waveguide Stasi[13] PPKTP Waveguide Vaidya[11] Si3N4 µ-ring This work PPLN µ-ring
1ps 1ps 1ps 1.5ns 300ps
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison table from one paper, partly of cited values, read from a flattened text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The mapping of numbers to rows relies on the flattened layer's order. The table's Stasi row gives the same g2, K and purity as this work, so the 99% purity is matched, not exceeded, by that source; this paper's chip advantage over it is the pump pulse length (300ps against 1ps), not purity. The table cites the Si3N4 ring as Vaidya[11] while reference [11] in the list is Morrison et al.; the mismatch is the paper's.

assertions.value: The authors list in Table II quality factors of N/A for the three waveguide sources and, as printed in the text layer, 8(105) for the Si3N4 microring and 1.15(105) for this work's microring.
assertions.certainty_reason: Read from a flattened table; the exponents are not recoverable from the layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The flat digits likely mean 8 times ten to the fifth and 1.15 times ten to the fifth; the exponent is not confirmable from the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that waveguide sources typically need picosecond pump pulses to match the filters for single modes, whereas resonator-based sources such as the present microrings can use pump pulses of a few hundred picoseconds to nanoseconds to match the cavity lifetime.
quotes: In waveguides, it typically requires to use picosecond pump pulses so as to match the optical filters for the generated photons, to obtain single modes.
the pump pulses can be much longer, ranging from a few hundred picoseconds to nanoseconds in order to match with the cavity’s lifetime for single modes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without a cited derivation in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state the pump pulses are made by a Highland Technology T130 EOM driver (250ps-30ns pulse width, 0-50MHz pulse rate) at 10MHz, amplified by an EDFA and frequency doubled in a bulk PPLN crystal, and report a measured photon-to-sync cross-correlation FWHM of around 320 ps, widened from the 300 ps electronic pulse by EO driver jitter (10 ps) and PNR-SNSPD jitter (54 ps).
quotes: a single-channel picosecond EOM (electro-optical modulator) driver (Highland Technology T130, 250ps-30ns pulse width, 0-50MHz pulse rate) supplies Radiofrequency pulse(10MHz) to the EOM.
The full width at half maximum is around 320 ps. Due to the EO Driver jitter(10 ps) and PNR-SNSPDs jitter(54 ps), it is slightly wider than the electronic pulse(300 ps).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own pump generation setup (Appendix A).

assertions.value: The authors claim the 27 MHz/µW brightness is among the highest across all SPDC sources in various materials, and that the detection rate is ten times higher than their previous result, which they ascribe to higher efficiencies in both photon pair generation and detection.
quotes: which is among the highest across all SPDC sources in various materials. The detection rate corresponds to ten times higher than our previous result [16]
we have scored a ten-fold enhancement in the SPDC generation rate of single-photon pairs [16]
obtained as the slope of the fitting curve as 27 MHz/µW
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparative claim; the paper gives no table of other sources' brightness.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper compares purity across sources in Table II but gives no brightness table, so the ranking among all SPDC sources is not checkable from this paper.

assertions.value: The authors claim to have performed coincident-to-accidental photon detection for multiphoton states using time-delayed measurement for the first time, and to have measured joint photon probabilities up to three photons in a channel.
quotes: We measured joint photon probabilities of multiphoton states up to three photons in a channel.
we have performed coincident to accidental photon detection for multiphoton states using time-delayed measurement, for the first time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A novelty claim with no literature survey in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, owing to subwavelength lateral confinement, the photons are created in single transverse modes of high purity, and that together with narrow cavity bandwidth the high purity and efficiency suppress background noise from, for example, Raman scattering or fluorescence emission.
quotes: Due to subwavelength lateral confinement, the photons are created in single transverse (spatial) modes of high purity.
Together with narrow cavity bandwidth, they suppress background noise created through, e.g., Raman scattering or fluorescence emission.
assertions.certainty_reason: Statements without a measurement of spatial-mode purity or noise in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no spatial-mode measurement and no noise-source measurement; the only measured purity is the time-frequency one from g2(0).

assertions.value: The authors state that in the joint-state calculation they neglect the contributions of detector dark counts and ambient photons, about 100 Hz.
quotes: where we neglect the contributions from detector dark counts and ambient photons (about 100 Hz)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own calculation (Photon correlation section).

assertions.value: The authors state that in bulk SPDC or four-wave mixing sources, putting multiphoton states in a single mode usually requires ultra-narrow band filtering or ultra-short broadband pump pulses, and that a third-order-nonlinearity microring was shown to produce squeezed states in good single modes but with parametric fluorescence emission into multiple cavity lines.
quotes: to meet this condition usually requires ultra-narrow band filtering or using ultra-short, broadband pump pulses [4, 9, 10]
albeit suffering parametric fluorescence emission into multiple cavity lines [11].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the PPLN microring is a SPDC source for multiphoton entanglement with both high efficiency and mode purity, that the work paves the way for advanced quantum photonic devices, and that they characterized photon statistics with a two-channel PNR-SNSPD system.
quotes: Our results highlight a SPDC source for multiphoton entanglement with both high efficiency and mode purity, as needed for many quantum information processing applications with multiphoton states.
This work paves the way for the development of advanced quantum photonic devices and systems with good performance and versatility.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper measures photon-number correlations and coincidences but does not report an entanglement measurement, so multiphoton entanglement is a prospective use here.
